Learning how to create an app in ChatGPT starts with the Jotform App Builder plugin (listed in ChatGPT's plugin directory as Jotform Apps): install it, connect a Jotform account, describe the app, approve the requested action, and refine the result. The plugin creates a Jotform App containing pages, forms, and resources that can be edited in Jotform App Builder and shared with its intended audience.

ChatGPT helps turn an idea into a clear request and supports revisions through conversation. The Jotform App Builder plugin performs the app-building actions, while the App Builder in Jotform provides the editor for closer customization.

This no-code ChatGPT app builder workflow suits projects built around information, forms, and everyday tasks.

"ChatGPT app development" can also describe coding projects. OpenAI's documentation on building plugins for ChatGPT describes a package of skills, an optional MCP server that connects to tools and data through the Model Context Protocol, optional UI, authentication, and publishing. The two routes differ like this:

This article covers the no-code route. The result is a Jotform App; the workflow does not include writing and deploying a separate codebase.

A Jotform App can organize pages, forms, and resources for customers, employees, members, or event attendees. The most useful first project has one audience and one clear purpose. Here are some examples:

These are starting structures. A booking form, for example, still needs its availability settings checked. An ordering app needs its order process reviewed, and any payment setup requires separate attention.

Setup starts with installing the plugin in ChatGPT and authorizing access to the intended Jotform account. Jotform's own how-to guide lists the steps.

To create an app in ChatGPT, select the installed plugin in a new chat and enter a specific description. Include the audience, purpose, pages, and design direction.

This gives the AI app builder a defined structure. The studio should then supply its real booking URL, approved resource links, contact details, and onboarding copy during review. It is important to review every generated form, link, and business rule before use.

A good prompt explains who will use the app, what they need to accomplish, and which elements support that task. Visual preferences help, but purpose and content should come first.

"Build an app for my business" leaves the audience, structure, and actions unclear. The design-studio example identifies a client audience, an onboarding task, specific pages, and a color scheme. Before submitting a request, define:

Request the essentials to build a Jotform App around one process, then expand.

The plugin supports follow-up requests in the same chat. Smaller changes make it easier to review each update and identify anything that needs correction. For the studio onboarding app, some follow-ups could include:

Each request should be followed by a review of the result. A map needs the correct address; a gallery needs suitable images; a booking form needs appropriate fields and configuration.

Select Edit in Jotform when you need closer editing. In Jotform App Builder, inspect every page, element, form, link, label, and visual choice. Replace the sample content and check that navigation follows the client's expected path. Third-party integrations require manual setup in the builder, so requesting a booking feature should not be treated as confirmation that an external calendar has been connected.

Select Share App in the generated result to open the available sharing options. For detailed distribution and access settings, open the app in Jotform App Builder and use the Publish tab and Quick Share. Jotform's sharing guide covers each option.

The builder supports copying the app link, inviting people by email, social sharing, and downloading a QR code. Choose the method that fits your audience: a client can receive a link, while event attendees may find a QR code more useful.

Review access before distributing the app, because newly created apps are public by default. Check exactly what a visitor can open before publishing.

Test the Jotform App as an intended user would, using fictional information first. Review it on both desktop and mobile before collecting real submissions.

Creating an app with the plugin is free to start, and Jotform offers a free Starter plan, but app usage remains subject to your account's allowances. A Jotform support reply from 2024 describes Starter as up to five forms and 100 monthly submissions. These are account allowances, rather than a separate allocation for each generated app, and they may have changed, so confirm them on Jotform's current pricing page. Paid plans provide more submissions.

Before you launch, compare expected usage with the current account limits. An onboarding app serving a few clients has different requirements from an event app collecting hundreds of registrations.

The most common mistakes are unclear requests, oversized first versions, and sharing before testing. Each can be reduced by defining a smaller task and reviewing the result.

This workflow is best for defined business tasks. Projects requiring extensive custom backend behavior need a separate assessment, such as the developer route described above.

Before sharing, confirm that the app serves its intended audience and that its content, behavior, and settings have been reviewed. A short launch checklist helps keep the review consistent.

#10336. Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold

A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.

The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.

The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.

A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959

In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.

In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.

Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.

The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.

Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.

These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.

The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.

Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.

How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment

The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.

Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.

The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.

The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.

By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.

Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.

Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution

The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.

Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.

Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.

Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.

"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."

What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.

A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion

With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.

Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.

When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.

Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.

The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.

This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.

The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.

A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics

The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.

The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.

Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.

Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.

By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.

The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.

The latest Steam Survey appears to show that gamers blessed with systems packing 32GB or more RAM and 1TB or more storage are a dwindling breed. This survey is posted without comment by Valve, as usual, but appears to show a significant proportional rise in gamers using 8GB and 16GB RAM PCs, which occurs largely at the expense of the 32GB brigade. The latest stats also show a noticeable increase in storage capacity poverty in the last month. Are the symptoms of the AI industry-induced components crunch now becoming evident among the PC gaming public?

The AI-pocalypse delivered components crunch has been in the headlines for months but it is still jarring to see it impact the vast PC gaming landscape. When we’ve browsed desktop and laptop PCs for the best gaming PC deals over the past months, the trend is clear. Systems that look like they are designed for gamers or enthusiasts are now frequently fitted with just 16GB of RAM as standard, and also feature smaller storage devices that one might have expected. But to see the Steam Survey suggesting that the share of 32GB systems has now collapsed by -5.16% is startling. Only last month, 32GB was the most popular configuration among gamers according to the same survey.

RAM is probably the hardest-hit component segment of AI-driven demand so far. We maintain a RAM price tracking page at Tom’s Hardware and the current state of the market means that DIYers or upgraders need to spend about $250 for 16GB DDR5 or $450 for 32GB DDR5. Those prices change regularly, as well.

Moving onto the sudden recorded change in storage configurations in use by Steam gamers, and we see that folks with 1TB of total fixed storage space or above shrunk by 4.68%. As the categories are currently defined, this appears to show the reduction in the number of systems coming with either a 2TB and 4TB SSD as standard. That’s because the 750GB to 999GB category grew +2.36%, and Windows registers a '1TB' boot disk as a smaller (a quick check shows ours at 924GB). 250GB to 499GB total storage systems were also up a similar amount (+2.30%). Overall, it looks like systems being used for Steam gaming are increasingly fitted with these smaller capacity SSDs. Enthusiasts, gamers, and DIYers wanting to expand their storage at the best prices are advised to keep an eye on our frequently updated SSD price tracking page.

We are currently seeing some extraordinary things in the GPU market, with reports of RTX 5090 and RTX 5080 cards being removed from retail. In the Steam Survey this month the RTX 5080 is still at position 14. However, the joint most popular GPUs are the RTX 5070 and the aging RTX 3060 – both with 3.78% of the market.

We are aware that there are sometimes some strong undercurrents in the Steam Survey that cause unusual fluctuations in the figures. However, the numbers this month don’t look like they have been impacted by a Chinese user or Chinese internet café PC influx, which have previously shown odd trends (such as a rise in Windows 10 usage). Actually, the Steam Survey shows Chinese (Simplified) language users surveyed are sharply down this month, so the survey should more accurately represent the system configurations typical among gamers in the West.

#10334. AssetOpsBench: Bridging the Gap Between AI Agent Benchmarks and Industrial Reality

AssetOpsBench is a comprehensive benchmark and evaluation system with six qualitative dimensions that bridges the gap for agentic AI in domain-specific settings, starting with industrial Asset Lifecycle Management.

While existing AI benchmarks excel at isolated tasks such as coding or web navigation, they often fail to capture the complexity of real-world industrial operations. To bridge this gap, we introduce AssetOpsBench, a framework specifically designed to evaluate agent performance across six critical dimensions of industrial applications. Unlike traditional benchmarks, AssetOpsBench emphasizes the need for multi-agent coordination—moving beyond `lone wolf' models to systems that can handle complex failure modes, integrate multiple data streams, and manage intricate work orders. By focusing on these high-stakes, multi-agent dynamics, the benchmark ensures that AI agents are assessed on their ability to navigate the nuances and safety-critical demands of a true industrial environment.

AssetOpsBench is built for asset operations such as chillers and air handling units. It comprises:

Experts helped curate 150+ scenarios. Each scenario includes metadata: task type, output format, category, and sub-agents. The tasks designed span across:

AssetOpsBench evaluates agentic systems across six qualitative dimensions designed to reflect real operational constraints in industrial asset management. Rather than optimizing for a single success metric, the benchmark emphasizes decision trace quality, evidence grounding, failure awareness, and actionability under incomplete and noisy data.

Each agent run is scored across six criteria:

Across early evaluations, we observe that many general-purpose agents perform well on surface-level reasoning but struggle with sustained multi-step coordination involving work orders, failure semantics, and temporal dependencies. Agents that explicitly model operational context and uncertainty tend to produce more stable and interpretable trajectories, even when final task completion is partial.

This feedback-oriented evaluation is intentional: in industrial settings, understanding why an agent fails is often more valuable than a binary success signal.

A central contribution of AssetOpsBench is the explicit treatment of failure modes as first-class evaluation signals in agentic industrial workflows. Rather than treating failure as a binary outcome, AssetOpsBench analyzes full multi-agent execution trajectories to identify where, how, and why agent behavior breaks down under realistic operational constraints.

Failure analysis in AssetOpsBench is implemented through a dedicated trajectory-level pipeline (TrajFM), which combines LLM-based reasoning with statistical clustering to surface interpretable failure patterns from agent execution traces. This pipeline operates in three stages: (1) trajectory-level failure extraction using an LLM-guided diagnostic prompt, (2) embedding-based clustering to group recurring failure patterns, and (3) analysis and visualization to support developer feedback and iteration.

Across industrial scenarios, recurrent failure modes include:

Importantly, AssetOpsBench does not rely solely on a fixed, hand-crafted failure taxonomy. While a structured set of predefined failure categories (e.g., verification errors, step repetition, role violations) is used for consistency, the system is explicitly designed to discover new failure patterns that emerge in practice. Additional failure modes identified by the LLM are embedded and clustered automatically, allowing the taxonomy to evolve as new agent designs and behaviors are evaluated.

To preserve industrial confidentiality, raw execution traces are never exposed. Instead, agents receive aggregated scores across six evaluation dimensions together with clustered failure-mode summaries that explain why an agent failed, without revealing sensitive data or intermediate reasoning steps. This feedback-driven design enables developers to diagnose weaknesses, refine agent workflows, and iteratively resubmit improved agents.

This failure-aware evaluation reflects the realities of industrial asset management, where cautious, degradation-aware reasoning—and the ability to recognize uncertainty, defer action, or escalate appropriately—is often preferable to aggressive but brittle automation.

To submit an agent, developers first validate their implementation locally using a provided simulated environment, which includes representative sensor data, work orders, alerts, and failure-mode catalogs. Agents are then containerized and submitted for remote execution on hidden evaluation scenarios.

Submitted agents are evaluated across six qualitative dimensions—task completion, accuracy, result verification, action sequencing, clarity, and hallucination—using a consistent, reproducible evaluation protocol. Execution traces are not exposed; instead, participants receive aggregated scores and structured failure-mode feedback that highlights where and why an agent’s reasoning or coordination broke down.

This feedback-driven evaluation loop enables iterative improvement: developers can diagnose failure patterns, refine agent design or workflow structure, and resubmit updated agents for further evaluation. Both planning-focused and execution-focused agents are supported, allowing researchers and practitioners to explore diverse agentic designs within the same benchmark framework.

This is an exceptionally important and well-executed benchmark. The shift in focus from "did the task succeed?" to "how and why did the process fail?" is precisely what's needed to move AI agents from research demos into high-stakes industrial environments.

The six-dimensional evaluation framework and the TrajFM pipeline for analyzing failure modes are standout contributions. The data you've shared is striking—particularly that no tested model, including the top performers, could meet the 85-point deployment readiness threshold. This honest result highlights a critical maturity gap and sets a clear, high bar for the community.

The findings around multi-agent coordination are especially valuable. The significant accuracy drop from single-agent (68%) to multi-agent (47%) workflows quantifies a major challenge many have anecdotally observed but rarely measured so clearly.

I have a couple of questions based on the thoughtful analysis:

Evolving Failure Taxonomy: You mention the system is designed to discover new failure patterns beyond the predefined taxonomy. Have you observed any novel, recurrent failure modes emerging from the community evaluations that are now being considered for inclusion in the core taxonomy?

Measuring Coordination Quality: The benchmark effectively captures that multi-agent coordination fails. Are there plans to develop more granular metrics to diagnose the quality of coordination itself (e.g., communication efficiency, conflict resolution) as a distinct dimension?

This is an open source project and you are more than welcome to contribute to the thoughtful analysis you have provided -Yes, for evolving failure mode, and we can add it to the core taxonomy.@mcemri / @melissapan Any suggestion?

I’ve been using AssetOpsBench in the context of industrial multi-agent evaluation, and what stands out to me is not just the benchmark itself, but the shift in mindset it represents. We finally have a structured way to stress-test coordination, orchestration, and tool reliability in Industry 4.0-style environments, instead of relying on isolated task accuracy.

In my own exploration, I’ve been particularly interested in:• Failure distributions across agent trajectories• Tool precision and recovery dynamics• Orchestration patterns under realistic industrial constraints• Governance implications for enterprise deployment

Is it smuggling if it's technically legal?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A memory smuggler has detailed how he gets export-controlled HBM chips from South Korea into China using a loophole. According to The Information, the smuggler owns a chip design firm that build cheap, low-performing processors that fall under the U.S. and South Korea’s export controls. They are then paired with expensive HBM from Samsung and SK hynix, that, on their own, are banned for export to China. But because export control rules only look at the performance of the server processor and not at the other components attached to it, this allows the HBM chips attached inside them to slip under the radar and make their way into China.

It’s not a risk-free operation, though. Once the mediocre processors with high-end memory chips land in Hong Kong and are smuggled across the border into Shenzhen in the luggage of commuters that cross between the two regions daily, they end up in workshops where technicians heat up the boards to soften the solder, gingerly lift the crucial memory chips, and discard the rest of the components. Despite having a high failure rate, the high price of HBM chips makes the procedure quite lucrative.

A Shenzhen-based chip broker has been making big money matching up suppliers such as the smuggler and companies that are desperate for HBM. “A year ago, a single HBM3E unit changed hands in China for several hundred dollars,” he tells the publication. “Today it’s about $4,000.” With an AI chip requiring six to eight high-end memory chips, that means the broker is raking in $24,000 to $32,000 for every AI GPU.

Chinese AI labs face this exact memory chip bottleneck when acquiring AI GPUs. While Chinese memory manufacturer CXMT has already begun risk production of HBM3E and is expected to mass produce them by the end of this year, it’s still reportedly suffering from low yield, which makes their chips expensive to produce and procure. We see this with Huawei’s Ascend 950DT, its current top-of-the-line processor that goes for about $37,000 — it offers similar pricing to Nvidia’s B200 AI GPU but only delivers half the performance of the previous-generation H100.

Huawei has reportedly said that its next-generation flagship AI processor, the 960DT, would deliver a similar performance as the H100. However, since the company cannot purchase HBM from Samsung and SK hynix, and Chinese memory manufacturers do not have the capacity to supply all its chip demands, Huawei told customers that they have to find the HBM that these servers need themselves. This would further fuel the demand for these chips, increase the price and make it more lucrative for smugglers to set up similar operations.

But given that this method of moving HBM chips into China is becoming more popular, the smuggler fears that South Korean and U.S. authorities would clamp down on their operations soon. Washington has been going down hard on activities like this, and we’ve seen high-profile arrests including some Super Micro executives and the CEO of a California-based tech company. Other countries like Taiwan and Malaysia have been ramping up their anti-smuggling activities, too, so it’s probably just a matter of time before Seoul follows suit.

#10331. Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations

Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.

The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.

The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.

Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.

Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.

Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.

The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.

"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.

"You just have to prepare it in the right way.

"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.

"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.

"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."

Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin

Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.

Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.

The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.

Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.

"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."

Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.

To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.

Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.

"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."

The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.

This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.

As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.

The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.

"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.

Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications

The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.

One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.

The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.

Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.

Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.

"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.

"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.

"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.

"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.

These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.

A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed

For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.

By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.

The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.

"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.

"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."

The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.

#10330. Unlocking Agentic RL Training for GPT-OSS: A Practical Retrospective

Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) extends traditional LLM training by optimizing not just a single-turn response, but an entire decision-making process learned through direct interaction with an environment during training. Unlike traditional single-turn reinforcement learning or offline preference-based methods that rely on static datasets, agentic RL trains policies by actively collecting on-policy data as the agent plans actions, invokes tools, observes outcomes, and adapts its behavior over multi-step trajectories in either simulated or real environments. This interaction-driven optimization assigns credit across long-horizon decisions, where intermediate choices such as query reformulation, tool selection, and execution order directly influence downstream success. Training follows an iterative closed loop in which the agent interacts with the environment to collect rollout trajectories, computes rewards over these trajectories, updates the policy based on observed outcomes, and then uses the updated policy to drive the next round of interaction and data collection such as GRPO or PPO algorithms..

LinkedIn is an AI-first company that's built agents to help professionals be more successful. In this setting, models must reason over incomplete information, interact with structured services, and adapt to evolving user intent across multiple steps rather than produce a single static response. These capabilities are especially critical for agents that support the goals of recruiters, job and knowledge seekers, and learners end users, such as retrieving information, refining queries, coordinating tools, and executing multi-step workflows. By learning robust decision policies through interaction, agentic RL provides a principled foundation for building scalable, reliable, and adaptable AI systems through end-to-end optimization.

The GPT-OSS model has shown comparable performance to OpenAI o3-mini and o4-mini [ref], but its suitability for agentic reinforcement learning training has not yet been validated. Most recent work focuses on fine-tuning without tool calling, such as: Fine-tuning with gpt-oss and Hugging Face Transformers and unsloth tutorial: how to fine-tune gpt-oss. This blog explores the journey to unlock agentic RL training for GPT-OSS as a potential backbone model for agentic applications.

In our experiments, we use verl as our training framework since it is one of the most popular adopted frameworks in the open source community. We use gsm8k, Retool task, verifiable instruction following task, which are commonly used in RL training. We focus on presenting experimental results for the GPT-OSS-20B model, and our attention-sink fix also works for GPT-OSS-120B. The Qwen-2.5-32B model is additionally used to benchmark standard metric trends during RL training.

verl has been an OSS framework used by the team, and the team has previously collaborated and contributed to it to help democratize agentic reinforcement learning training. With the introduction of the new Harmony chat template in GPT-OSS, the first step is to ensure that the training framework fully supports the updated message format and conversation semantics required by Harmony. This step helps rollout generation, trajectory construction, and tool parsing remain consistent and correct under the new template.

The team uses ReTool as a representative example to verify code correctness. ReTool is an agentic coding task in which the model is asked to solve a math problem with the assistance of a code compiler tool. This setup allows the model to focus on core reasoning and algorithmic logic, while delegating the actual arithmetic and execution to the tool. During an episode, the model interacts with the code tool multiple times, using execution results as feedback to refine its solution. At the end of the trajectory, the model produces a final answer, on which the reward is computed.

During the initial training runs, we observed exploding KL divergence and entropy, along with non-increasing rewards, indicating underlying issues in the GPT-OSS training setup, as shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1. Left: Qwen32b has significantly higher rewards compared to GPT-OSS 20B; Right: The gradient norm exploded as training progressed.

Figure 2. Non-zero importance sampling clip value even for on-policy training.

We focus on on-policy methods because they provide greater stability and more reliable convergence. The foundation of pure on-policy Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) mandates that the importance sampling ratio must be exactly 1. The mathematical definition of the importance ratio is:

ratio=π(a∣s)πold(a∣s) \text{ratio} = \frac{\pi(a \mid s)}{\pi_{\text{old}}(a \mid s)} ratio=πold​(a∣s)π(a∣s)​

This requirement ensures that the policy update is executed only on the data generated by the current policy π(a | s) = πold(a | s), preventing unintended clipping.

We have observed the non-zero clipping value in our ReTool training, as shown in Figure 2, stemming from a mismatch between the two log-probabilities:

Root Cause: The Dual Forward Pass and MoE Architecture

Prior to verl 0.3.0, the implementation relied on two separate forward passes (one to compute the current log_prob and one to retrieve the stored old_log_prob) for the same state-action pair.

In a Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture like GPT-OSS, the gating network routes the input to different experts. Due to implementation factors (e.g., subtle floating-point differences or explicit stochasticity), the expert routing can differ slightly between the two passes. Readers who are interested can further read Stabilizing MoE Reinforcement Learning by Aligning Training and Inference Routers.

log⁡(π(a∣s))≠log⁡(πold(a∣s)) \log(\pi(a \mid s)) \neq \log(\pi_{\text{old}}(a \mid s)) log(π(a∣s))=log(πold​(a∣s))

The resulting ratio deviates from 1, falsely triggering the PPO clip and violating the core on-policy assumption.

Solution: Enforcing Ratio = 1 via Log-Probability Substitution

The fix resolves the issue by logically overriding the flawed computation when the environment is known to be on-policy (i.e., when the minibatch size equals the global batch size):

By setting old_log_prob equal to the newly computed log_prob (detached to prevent gradient flow through the reference value), the importance ratio is mathematically forced back to 1. This strategy bypasses the instability caused by MoE's non-deterministic routing and guarantees strict on-policy behavior during PPO training.

Although fixing the log-probability mismatch reduced the importance-sampling clip ratio to zero, gradient norms continued to explode and rewards failed to improve. To isolate the issue, we simplified training to GSM8K, a single-step task without agentic tool use. The same instability persisted, as shown in the green curves in Figure 3, indicating a fundamental issue in basic RL training with GPT-OSS under verl.

We hypothesize that training–inference mismatch could be a potential cause: discrepancies between inference-time execution—where engines such as vLLM and SGLang aggressively optimize for throughput—and training-time execution under FSDP, which prioritizes numerical precision and stability, can effectively turn otherwise on-policy RL into off-policy optimization.

This blog details why such mismatches lead to unstable gradients and non-improving rewards. Figure 3 compares training runs with and without rollout correction (see this verl blog for details). After applying rollout correction, training dynamics improve significantly, with gradient norms remaining stable rather than exploding.

However, as shown in the left plot of Figure 4, the reward increases only modestly, and convergence on the simple GSM8K task remains substantially slower compared to smaller dense model variants.

Figure 3. Gradient norm behavior under different training configurations. Green: Training without rollout correction, exhibiting unstable gradients. Red: Training with the attention layer frozen to isolate the issue to the attention mechanism, resulting in partial stabilization. Blue: Training with rollout correction enabled (sequence-level importance sampling), yielding stable gradient norms.

Figure 4. Left: Reward improvement on GSM8K remains slow even after applying rollout correction, with performance comparable to runs where the attention layer is frozen during training. Right: A substantial log-ppl mismatch is observed between the inference engine (SGLang with Triton kernels supporting attention-sink forward passes) and the training stack (FSDP with FlashAttention-v2), indicating a large training–inference inconsistency.

To further isolate the root cause, we freeze the attention layers during training and observe reward dynamics similar to those of runs without freezing (blue curve vs yellow curve in Figure 4). This indicates that learning is primarily driven by the MoE layers, while the attention mechanism contributes less effectively than expected. In addition, we observe a substantial token-level probability mismatch between the inference engine and the distributed training stack which are using different attention kernels. Together, these observations motivate a deeper investigation into the attention mechanism.

Attention sinks used in GPT-OSS are learnable scalar parameters (one per attention head) that act as "virtual tokens" in the softmax computation. They allow the model to allocate attention mass to a learned sink rather than forcing all attention to content tokens, which has been shown to improve attention stability in streaming inference and training with sliding-window attention.

After a deeper investigation, we identified several major issues:

Key difference: The sink participates in softmax normalization but doesn't contribute to the output.

The attention weight for content token j in row i is defined as:

Pij=exp⁡(Sij)∑j′=1Nkexp⁡(Sij′)+exp⁡(Sh) P_{ij} = \frac{\exp(S_{ij})} {\sum_{j'=1}^{N_k} \exp(S_{ij'}) + \exp(S_h)} Pij​=∑j′=1Nk​​exp(Sij′​)+exp(Sh​)exp(Sij​)​

The sink probability is computed but not used in the output:

Pi,h=exp⁡(Sh)∑j′=1Nkexp⁡(Sij′)+exp⁡(Sh) P_{i,h} = \frac{\exp(S_h)} {\sum_{j'=1}^{N_k} \exp(S_{ij'}) + \exp(S_h)} Pi,h​=∑j′=1Nk​​exp(Sij′​)+exp(Sh​)exp(Sh​)​

The gradient of the loss L with respect to the sink parameter Sh is:

∂L∂Sh=−∑iPi,h(∂L∂Si,h−∑j∈{1,…,Nk}Pij∂L∂Sij) \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_h} = - \sum_i P_{i,h} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_{i,h}} - \sum_{j \in \{1,\ldots,N_k\}} P_{ij} \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_{ij}} \right) ∂Sh​∂L​=−i∑​Pi,h​​∂Si,h​∂L​−j∈{1,…,Nk​}∑​Pij​∂Sij​∂L​​

Since the sink is computed but not used in the output, its gradient ∂L/∂Si,h = 0.

Therefore, the backward equation simplifies to:

∂L∂Sh=−∑iPi,h(∑j∈{1,…,Nk}Pij∂L∂Sij) \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_h} = - \sum_i P_{i,h} \left( \sum_{j \in \{1,\ldots,N_k\}} P_{ij} \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_{ij}} \right) ∂Sh​∂L​=−i∑​Pi,h​​j∈{1,…,Nk​}∑​Pij​∂Sij​∂L​​

The forward pass was adapted from vLLM's FlashAttention fork, and we implemented the backward pass to compute gradients for the sink parameters. The implementation will be released following the internal review process.

After applying the fix in FlashAttention v3, we observe substantially faster convergence for GPT-OSS-20B across a range of reinforcement learning tasks. These include single-turn RL on math reasoning (GSM8K — red curve in Figure 5), instruction following (VerifyIf, evaluated on an out-of-domain multi-if benchmark — Figure 6), and multi-turn agentic RL with tool use (ReTool — Figure 7).

Across all settings, training becomes stable and exhibits steady reward improvement.

Figure 5.. Single Turn GSM8K, the red curve converges much faster than the rest without the fix

Figure 6. On verifiable instruction following the task, the run without the fix collapsed (blue), and the run with fix showed steady reward improvement.

Figure 7. On the Retool task, the run with fix showed steady reward improvement and no gradient exploding (fa2 is the flash attention 2 without the fix while fa3 is the flash attention 3 with the fix). After the fix, the validation accuracy score goes up now.

One issue we consistently encountered was excessive memory allocation during the FSDP forward pass, which led to repeated out-of-memory (OOM) failures when training GPT-OSS-20B bf16 models on 16 H200 nodes (max response length: 16k, prompt length: 8k). This behavior is highly unexpected for a 20B-parameter MoE model.

We identified the issue as originating from two different implementations of the MoE forward path in Hugging Face Transformers. This issue has also been reported by other users: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/40073; When verl computes log-probabilities under FSDP, the inference forward path is triggered. In the current Hugging Face implementation, this path duplicates hidden states for all experts and performs batched matrix multiplication, materializing extremely large tensors in GPU memory. By contrast, the training forward path uses a for-loop to process each expert sequentially and then combines the results. While slower, this approach is significantly more memory efficient.

We patched the Hugging Face implementation to use a more memory-efficient execution path, avoiding repeated materialization of experts.

Agentic RL requires the agent to interact with the environment over multiple steps while maintaining an ever-expanding context. Observations and environment feedback from each step are appended to the context and used as input for subsequent decision-making, which introduces significant challenges for memory efficiency and scalability during training.

Under fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), model parameters, optimizer states, and gradients are sharded across the entire world size (i.e., all GPUs in the training cluster). Each GPU stores and updates only its assigned parameter shards, while rollout data are replicated across all GPUs—meaning every GPU processes the full agent interaction history for each rollout.

During the forward pass, when computation reaches a layer whose parameters are not locally available, an all_gather operation is triggered to materialize the full parameters across GPUs. During the backward pass, a corresponding reduce_scatter operation aggregates gradients and ensures that each GPU retains only its local shard. This provides a degree of scaling: as the number of GPUs increases, the per-GPU memory footprint decreases.

FSDP provides model-level scaling by sharding model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across GPUs. Sequence parallelism (or context parallelism) further reduces per-GPU memory consumption by partitioning the input sequence across devices, thereby lowering the peak activation memory on each GPU.

As the number of sequence-parallel dimensions increases, the maximum activation memory per GPU correspondingly decreases. We have implemented sequence parallelism to be attention-sink-aware and compatible with FlashAttention v3 (Figure 8, right).

Figure 8. Left: Inference without sequence parallelism. Right: Inference with sequence parallelism, where additional all-to-all communication is performed before and after the attention layer. This partitions the sequence across parallel workers and reduces the peak memory footprint of attention computation by a factor proportional to the sequence-parallelism degree.

Sequence parallelism scales along the sequence dimension to reduce the per-GPU activation footprint. Input tokens from all sequences are packed into a single contiguous list by removing padding tokens, while position IDs are used to distinguish tokens belonging to different sequences. This design naturally benefits from FlashAttention’s variable-length support. For sequence parallelism, layers other than the attention layer do not have inter-position dependencies; therefore, they do not require each GPU to hold a complete sequence shard, and no additional communication is needed for these layers.

The attention layer, however, requires all tokens belonging to the same sequence to be present on the same GPU in order to compute attention weights correctly. To satisfy this constraint, an all-to-all communication is performed to gather sequence elements, with the split performed at the attention-head level. This design avoids communication within the attention computation itself, which would otherwise be prohibitively expensive. After the attention layer, a single all-to-all communication redistributes the outputs back to their original sequence-parallel layout, after which the remaining non-attention layers can proceed without further synchronization.

Our journey to enable agentic RL training for the GPT-OSS backbone model was a practical retrospective, highlighting that unlocking advanced capabilities in open-source LLMs requires meticulous, deep-dive engineering.

We made contributions that transformed the viability of GPT-OSS for agentic applications, specifically by:

Stabilizing PPO: We contributed a fix to restore on-policy integrity, overriding the log-probability mismatch caused by the MoE architecture’s non-determinism (Figure 2).

Enabling Attention Sink Support: We successfully implemented and integrated the attention sink backward pass into FlashAttention v3, correcting the catastrophic training–inference mismatch that had previously caused instability and slow convergence (Figures 5, 6, and 7).

Scaling Memory Efficiency: We introduced crucial memory optimizations, including patching the MoE materialization process and integrating sequence parallelism with the new attention sink support, enabling training with the long context windows essential for multi-step agents (Figure 8).

These engineering efforts validate GPT-OSS as a scalable and high-performance backbone for building the next generation of intelligent, multi-step decision-making agents.

Thanks to Deepak Agarwal, Bee-Chung Chen, Animesh Singh, Gungor Polatkan, Balaji Krishnapuram, and Jitendra Agarwal for their leadership support.

Thank you for this detailed retrospective on enabling agentic RL training for GPT-OSS. The article clearly documents important challenges and practical solutions. I have a few questions and observations that might help clarify some aspects.

Mathematical Clarification on Attention Sink Gradient

Regarding the attention sink backward pass derivation (Section 4), I'd appreciate clarification on the notation and justification. The article presents the general formula: ∂L/∂S_h = -Σ_i P_{i,h} (∂L/∂S_{i,h} - Σ_{j∈{1,...,N_k}} P_{ij} ∂L/∂S_{ij}). Then states that ∂L/∂S_{i,h} = 0 because "the sink is computed but not used in the output," leading to the simplified form: ∂L/∂S_h = -Σ_i P_{i,h} (Σ_j P_{ij} ∂L/∂S_{ij}).

I believe the final formula is correct, but the notation ∂L/∂S_{i,h} is unclear. If this refers to the gradient of the loss with respect to the sink's contribution to the output at position i (i.e., ∂L/∂(P_{i,h} V_sink)), then indeed it would be zero since there's no V_sink term. However, the sink parameter S_h itself does affect the output through softmax normalization: P_{ij} = exp(S_{ij}) / (Σ_{j'} exp(S_{ij'}) + exp(S_h)). When S_h changes, all P_{ij} change, affecting O_i = Σ_j P_{ij} V_j. The gradient ∂L/∂S_h is non-zero and flows through this normalization.

Could you clarify what ∂L/∂S_{i,h} represents in your notation? Also, could you provide the full derivation showing how you arrive at the final form from the chain rule through the softmax operation? A step-by-step derivation would help readers verify the implementation and understand how the gradient flows through the attention mechanism.

The solution for the MoE log-probability mismatch (Section 2) sets old_log_prob = log_prob.detach() when on_policy=True. While this mathematically forces the importance sampling ratio to 1, I'm curious about the implications. If the policy parameters change between rollout collection and the training step (even slightly), this fix would still assume ratio = 1. How do you ensure true on-policy conditions? Do you collect rollouts and train in the same step, or is there a mechanism to detect policy drift?

Have you considered storing the actual routing decisions during rollout to ensure deterministic replay, or using deterministic routing during training? This might address the root cause rather than working around it. Also, the fix only applies when on_policy=True. How do you handle cases where the policy has drifted? Is there a threshold or mechanism to detect when to switch to off-policy mode?

Several aspects would benefit from additional detail. Which fix had the largest impact? Are all three fixes necessary, or would fixing attention sinks alone have been sufficient? A table showing results with/without each fix would be very helpful. You mention the fixes work for GPT-OSS-120B, but no experimental results are shown. Could you share learning curves or metrics for the 120B model?

The article mentions both vLLM and SGLang. Which engine is used for rollouts in the final experiments? If different engines are used for different experiments, how does this affect the training-inference mismatch analysis? You also reference "rollout correction (sequence-level importance sampling)" and mention "this verl blog," but the details aren't explained. Could you clarify what this correction does and how it relates to the attention sink fix?

The article mentions that "The implementation will be released following the internal review process." For reproducibility and verification, it would be valuable to know an approximate timeline for release, whether the backward pass implementation will be contributed to the main FlashAttention repository, and if there are any interim workarounds or partial implementations that could be shared.

Despite these questions, the article makes valuable contributions. It clearly identifies real-world challenges with MoE + RL training, documents the engineering journey transparently, shows substantial improvements in training stability, and raises awareness of training-inference mismatch issues. The fixes appear to work well for your use case, and the results demonstrate clear improvements. My questions are aimed at understanding the details better and ensuring the solutions are robust and reproducible.

Thank you again for sharing this work with the community!

You confirmed that forcing old_log_prob = log_prob.detach() does not resolve the on-policy issue: the evaluation uses the current policy π(a|s), but the sampling distribution can still differ because expert selection at rollout time can differ from the training forward pass. Forcing the importance ratio to 1 in the PPO formula therefore doesn't fix the underlying problem—the data can still be effectively off-policy. I agree with that distinction.

You clarified the debugging sequence: root cause was unknown at first; you hypothesized inference–training inconsistency; importance sampling (rollout correction) didn't fix it; then you tried forcing the detach as a hypothesis test to see whether the MoE log-prob mismatch was the cause. That makes it clear the detach was diagnostic, not the actual fix.

You noted that expert router replay wasn't available in verl when you were debugging; you've since tested it (Stabilizing MoE RL, arxiv 2510.11370) and it was not the root cause—the root cause is attention sink. That fits the story: the real mismatch is at the attention layer (training on FA2 without sink support vs. inference on sink-aware kernels), so token-level log-probs diverge between rollout and training. That explains why rollout correction alone didn't fix things (it corrects at sequence level but not at the attention computation) and why freezing attention gave similar reward curves (attention wasn't learning correctly without the sink backward). I'm satisfied on the on-policy/MoE part.

What wasn't addressed: You addressed the MoE/on-policy part; the following from my original comment were not covered. If you have bandwidth, they would help for implementation and reproducibility:

The article gives the general form∂L/∂S_h = -Σ_i P_{i,h} (∂L/∂S_{i,h} - Σ_j P_{ij} ∂L/∂S_{ij}),then states that ∂L/∂S_{i,h} = 0 because "the sink is computed but not used in the output," yielding∂L/∂S_h = -Σ_i P_{i,h} Σ_j P_{ij} ∂L/∂S_{ij}.

Definition of ∂L/∂S_{i,h}: In the extended softmax, the logits are (S_{i,1}, …, S_{i,N_k}, S_h). The output is O_i = Σ_j P_{ij} V_j with no V_sink term, so the sink affects O_i only through the normalization Z_i = Σ_{j'} exp(S_{ij'}) + exp(S_h). The direct contribution of the sink to the output (e.g. a P_{i,h} V_sink term) is therefore zero, so ∂L/∂S_{i,h} in that sense is 0. If ∂L/∂S_{i,h} is defined differently in your derivation, a one-sentence definition in the article would remove ambiguity.

Chain rule through softmax: A short derivation showing how ∂L/∂S_h is obtained from ∂L/∂P_{ij} (and possibly ∂L/∂O_i) via ∂P_{ij}/∂S_h and ∂P_{i,h}/∂S_h would let readers verify the sign and aggregation over query positions i and match it to the FlashAttention backward API.

To reproduce and extend the results, it would be helpful to have:

Ablation: Was the FA3 + sink backward sufficient for stable training (with MoE materialization and sequence parallelism only for correctness/memory), or did you still rely on rollout correction or the on-policy detach in the final runs? A small table (e.g. FA2 vs FA3+sink, with/without rollout correction) would make the relative impact clear.

Rollout engine: The article mentions both vLLM and SGLang; Figure 4 references SGLang with Triton kernels for the sink forward. Which engine was used for rollouts in the final experiments (Figures 5–7), and was it the same across GSM8K, VerifyIf, and ReTool? This matters for training–inference consistency.

Rollout correction vs sink fix: A one-sentence summary of what "rollout correction" (sequence-level importance sampling) does in your pipeline and whether it is still enabled in the FA3+sink runs would clarify how the two mechanisms interact.

GPT-OSS-120B: You mention the sink fix also works for 120B; any learning curves or metrics (even high-level) would be valuable for scaling.

For verification and adoption: any update on timeline for releasing the sink backward implementation, whether you plan to contribute it to the main FlashAttention repo or keep it in a fork, and whether there are interim options (e.g. a reference PyTorch implementation or a patch description) would help the community reproduce the results and align training with inference.

Thanks again for the clarification; the narrative (hypothesis testing → rollout correction → attention sink as root cause) is much clearer, and the work is clearly valuable for agentic RL on GPT-OSS.

Will you release the weights of the gpt-oss-agentic models you trained? I'm sure they'd be very popular.

Learning to code can feel overwhelming at first. There are different programming languages, development tools, and concepts to understand, and choosing where to begin is not always easy. Coding apps can make the process more approachable by breaking lessons into smaller steps and giving beginners a place to practice what they learn.

Whether you want to build websites, develop software, or explore programming as a new skill, the right app can help you get started. Some platforms focus on interactive lessons, while others offer coding exercises, guided projects, or access to a full development environment.

Here are six coding apps worth considering if you're learning programming for the first time.

Mimo is a beginner-friendly coding app designed to help users learn programming through short lessons and interactive exercises. Rather than starting with lengthy explanations, it introduces concepts in manageable steps, making it easier to fit learning into a busy schedule.

The app covers several topics, including Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and SQL. This makes it useful for beginners who want to explore general programming or focus on web development. As learners progress, they can work through structured learning paths and practice applying concepts through coding exercises and projects.

Mimo is particularly suitable for people who prefer a guided learning experience instead of figuring out what to study next on their own. Its mobile-first approach also makes it convenient to practice during breaks or while traveling.

A free starting option is available, although access to some courses and features requires a paid plan.

Best for: Beginners who want structured lessons and practical coding exercises.

SoloLearn is a coding education platform that helps beginners explore programming languages through short lessons, quizzes, and hands-on practice. It is a useful starting point for people who want to understand programming fundamentals before committing to a specific development path.

The platform offers courses in languages and technologies such as Python, JavaScript, Java, C++, SQL, HTML, and CSS. Its bite-sized lessons make complicated topics easier to approach, while interactive exercises let learners test their understanding as they progress.

Another useful feature is its learning community, where users can explore other people's code, participate in discussions, and learn from different approaches to programming problems.

SoloLearn works well for people who are still deciding which language to learn. However, completing lessons alone is not enough to develop strong programming skills. Beginners should also practice writing their own programs and building small projects.

The platform offers free learning options alongside paid features.

Best for: Beginners who want to explore multiple programming languages and learn through short, interactive lessons.

Codecademy Go is the mobile companion to Codecademy's online learning platform. It is designed to help learners reinforce programming concepts and review material while away from their computers.

Codecademy's broader learning platform offers courses covering web development, Python, JavaScript, SQL, and other technical subjects. The mobile app can be useful for reviewing concepts, practicing through supported activities, and maintaining a consistent learning routine between longer study sessions.

For example, someone taking a JavaScript course on a computer can use the mobile experience to revisit concepts and strengthen their understanding before returning to practical exercises.

It is important to distinguish between learning on a mobile device and developing software on one. Codecademy Go is primarily a companion for learning and review rather than a complete replacement for a desktop coding environment.

Some learning content is available without a subscription, while access to additional courses and features depends on the current plan.

Best for: Learners who want to review programming concepts alongside a structured online course.

Programming Hub is an educational app for people who want to explore programming and related technical subjects in one place. It brings together lessons, examples, and exercises designed to introduce users to different areas of software development.

Its learning material covers languages such as Python, Java, C++, and JavaScript, along with web development and other computing topics. This variety can be helpful for beginners who want to compare different languages before choosing one to study in depth.

The app's lesson-based approach makes it possible to explore a topic without immediately installing a development environment or configuring complicated software. Code examples and practice activities can also help learners connect theoretical concepts with practical applications.

However, beginners should avoid jumping between too many languages at once. Starting with one language, understanding its fundamentals, and applying those skills to a small project will generally provide a stronger foundation.

Programming Hub offers free and paid options, with access depending on the selected plan.

Best for: Beginners who want an introduction to several programming languages and computing topics.

Enki takes a slightly different approach to learning programming by emphasizing regular practice and the development of technical skills over time. Its lessons and exercises are designed to help users strengthen their understanding through consistent, manageable learning sessions.

Depending on the learning content available, users can explore topics such as Python, SQL, JavaScript, data analysis, and other areas of technology. This makes the app relevant to both aspiring developers and people who want to improve their technical knowledge for work.

One advantage of short, recurring practice sessions is that they encourage learners to revisit concepts instead of studying them once and moving on. Regular revision can help reinforce programming syntax, terminology, and problem-solving techniques.

Enki may be especially useful for people who already have some exposure to coding and want to maintain a learning habit. Complete beginners should check whether the available lessons match their chosen language and current skill level before starting.

The app offers different access options, so check its current listing for details about free and paid features.

Best for: Learners who prefer regular practice and gradual improvement in technical skills.

Replit is a browser-based development platform that allows users to write, run, and test code without setting up a traditional development environment on their computer. It is particularly useful for beginners who want to move beyond lessons and start creating their own programs.

Users can work with languages and technologies such as Python, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, depending on the project and environment. Instead of only answering quiz questions, learners can experiment with code, identify errors, and see how their changes affect a working application.

For example, a beginner learning Python could create a simple calculator, while someone studying web development could build a basic personal website. Starting with small projects helps learners understand how individual programming concepts work together.

Replit also provides AI-assisted development features, which can help users explore ideas and understand code. However, beginners should review generated code and learn why it works rather than relying on automated suggestions without understanding them.

Replit offers a free starting option, with additional capabilities available through paid plans. Features and usage limits may vary.

Best for: Beginners who want to practice writing code and experiment with real projects in a development environment.

The best coding app depends on your learning goals, preferred learning style, and current experience. Before choosing one, consider what you want to accomplish.

Choose a language first. If you want to learn general programming, Python is a reasonable starting point. If your goal is to build websites, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are more directly relevant.

Consider how you learn. Apps such as Mimo and SoloLearn emphasize short lessons and interactive practice. Codecademy Go is useful for reviewing course material, while Replit provides an environment for experimenting with code.

Look for practical exercises. Understanding a lesson is only the beginning. Choose resources that encourage you to write code, solve problems, and apply concepts in small projects.

Check the cost. Several coding apps provide free introductory content, but some courses and advanced features may require subscriptions. Review the current pricing before committing to a paid plan.

Move beyond the app. As your skills improve, practice using a computer, read technical documentation, and create projects of your own. These activities help you develop the problem-solving skills required for real programming work.

Coding apps provide an accessible way to begin learning programming without needing extensive technical knowledge or complicated software installations. They can help you understand basic concepts, practice regularly, and discover which areas of development interest you most.

Mimo and SoloLearn are worth exploring if you prefer guided lessons, while Codecademy Go can complement a structured course. Programming Hub and Enki offer alternative approaches to learning and practice, and Replit provides a way to experiment with working code.

You do not need to master every programming language or use several apps simultaneously. Start with one resource, focus on a single learning goal, and gradually apply what you learn to practical projects. Consistent practice and curiosity will take you further than simply completing lessons.

#10328. AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious

Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).

As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?

New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.

How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness

Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.

"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.

"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."

To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.

Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.

A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness

The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.

However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.

The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.

"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."

Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.

The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.

Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.

Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.

The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.

"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."
